title: Do Decodables Promote Love of Reading? What Books Launch Lifetime Readers?
author: Timothy Shanahan
summary: Responding to a K-3 teacher who worries that a diet of decodable texts will stop children loving reading, Timothy Shanahan first concedes that no study answers the question directly. He then draws on what research does show about young readers' choices: beginners are motivated chiefly by the experience of being able to read, so simple books such as Tug the Pup can satisfy them as much as Caldecott winners. Reviewing the preference literature, he finds that studies on fiction versus nonfiction or fantasy versus realism contradict one another, and he reads that as evidence that people read for many different reasons, including information, escape, belonging and pride. His practical advice is not to fret about whether children enjoy their decodables, to keep such texts plentifully available for self-selected reading, and to remember that decodables make pedagogical sense only for a brief period and never as the only reading. The larger goal, he argues, is to teach children why people read and how to choose texts for different purposes.
points: For beginning readers the motivator is the feeling of competence at reading, which is why they happily reread and choose short, easy books that let them finish.
Preference studies conflict on fiction versus nonfiction and fantasy versus realism, which shows there is no single reason to read and no single text type that creates lifelong readers.
Decodables should stay available for self-selected reading, since many children enjoy them and report liking reading more after phonics work, but they should never be the only diet.
Reading choices are shaped by availability, awareness, covers, series, friends and social belonging, so schools should widen access and exposure rather than debate book merit alone.
Teach children why people read and which texts serve which purposes, not only how to decode.
quotes: What turns on beginning readers? Being able to read! They want to be successful, competent, and effective; grown up.

The researcher assumed that the books themselves were the main feature of these kids’ reading, that the kids read for the books. That’s not the case for most beginners and probably not for many of the rest of us either.

My point isn’t that kids’ choices should be limited to decodables or books with lots of repeated vocabulary. But those choices should be copiously available for self-selected reading given how successfully they fulfill kids’ desires and needs.
Unfortunately, this is one of those “there’s no research on that” questions. No studies have set out to provide any direct and definitive answer to your query.

My point – and the ultimate contribution of this collection of studies – is that there is not a single reason to read. Accordingly, there isn’t one kind of text that will encourage kids to love reading and want to engage in it.
Decodables make pedagogical sense for a brief period, but never as the only things kids should be reading even during that period.
Kids should learn not just how to read, but why people read, and what kinds of texts they read to accomplish their multiplicity of goals, and how to successfully handle that plethora of text types.
